utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Dr. Parsons. If I could just ask you to please state your name for the record so we have it.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS

I'd like to start with a bit of your background, if I could. So I'd like to ask you, first, if you could just briefly tell us what is your educational background.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I have a bachelor's degree in physics from the University of Chicago. A PhD in biochemistry from the University of Washington in the United States and extensive post-doctoral experience in molecular evolution and DNA population genetics at the Smithsonian Institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you tell us a little bit about your professional experience up until you started working for the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: My relevant professional experience specifically in forensic DNA began in 1994 when I joined the US Armed Forces DNA Identification Laboratory that was pioneering new techniques to identify the mortal remains of missing service personnel from Vietnam. In 2006, I joined the International Commission on Missing Persons as the director of forensic sciences.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you indicated that you've done some post-doctoral work. Was that specific to DNA analysis?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And prior to your testimony in this case, have you testified as an expert or been so qualified before either this Tribunal or any other court with respect to DNA analysis or DNA evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just before I get into the details of what your work is there, your duties and responsibilities, I'd like to ask you a couple of questions about the ICMP itself and I'd like to start with first asking you about what the ICMP's mission is. If you could briefly acquaint the Court with that.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The ICMP was established in 2006 with the mandate to assist governments with dealing with issues of missing persons. It is an independent, non-governmentally aligned body that seeks the co-operation of governments in helping them to resolve all the aspects that are associated with missing persons cases and societal impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Does the ICMP engage in any kind of civil society initiatives or provide assistance to governments or other forensic institutions, for example, with respect to DNA identifications?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: There are three primary activities that the ICMP engages in, if one would class it very generally. The first would be to assist political and institutional processes for the state to accept responsibility for the issues of the missing, including their identification. The second would be to work with families who are badly affected by the issue of missing persons, very often supporting family organisations and encouraging them to have a voice in national affairs. And then lastly, there is extensive provision of forensic science expertise to assist with the identification of the missing as well as the recovery of the missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you could, could you outline the basic structure of the organisation for us?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: In our activities in the Western Balkans, we have a primary political unit that is headed by the ICMP director-general. We have a justice and civil society initiatives unit that deals primarily with family issues and societal issues. And we have a Forensic Science Division, of which -- that I supervise that consists itself of three different areas. The first is archaeology and anthropology with regard to the recovery and examination of human remains. The second is an Identification Co-ordination Division which accepts samples for DNA testing and distributes them to the third division, which is the DNA laboratory system where DNA profiles are obtained from both family members of the missing and human remains that have been recovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In terms of the DNA analysis activities of the ICMP, can you tell us where and what locations or areas the ICMP has been engaged?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia we've been engaged throughout the entire country of Bosnia and Herzegovina, having numerous facilities over the years and assisted at hundreds and hundreds of recovery reconnaissance and exhumation activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us about -- okay. Sorry. Let me start again. Where is the ICMP currently engaged?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: We are currently headquartered in Sarajevo, in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We do work now globally, both with missing from armed conflict as well as disaster victim identification on an ad hoc basis. So we maintain offices in Erbil and Baghdad in Iraq as well now as in Tripoli in Libya.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is the organisation involved in performing DNA analysis with respect to conflicts ongoing in those areas or other things, disasters and so on?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Indeed. We conduct DNA analysis from cases in Iraq and Libya in addition to a comprehensive programme of training in archaeology, anthropology, and the design and execution of an in-country DNA identification capability. With regard to disaster victim identification, we have been involved in quite a number of incidents worldwide. A large ferry disaster in the Philippines. The 2004 South-East Asian tsunami, Hurricane Katrina in the United States, and a number of plane crashes and other incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In conducting these activities, to whom is the organisation accountable?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: We conduct our work through agreement with partner agencies, and with regard to accountability, the ICMP's upper echelon of management and direction is the International Commission on Missing Persons. The commissioners are notable diplomats and other societal luminaries who overall direct and supervise the conduct of the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about the role and the function of the Steering Committee on Forensic Sciences Programs at the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The forensic work that is conducted by the ICMP is quite sophisticated and indeed quite complex and has caused us in many instances to work at the forefront of capabilities and applications in this field. Commensurate with that, we have sought to continually interact with other experts in the world to make sure that we are accessing the best techniques as well as make sure that our methods are well communicated to the global scientific community, understood, and then also vetted as appropriate and rigorous. One of the many tools that we employ in that regard is a standing Steering Committee on Forensic Science Programs that represents some dozen or so experts in many of the subdisciplines where the ICMP is engaged, and they meet annually with the ICMP as well as on an ad hoc basis as consultant experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us a little bit about the advisory committee of government representatives?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Vanderpuye, I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Does the ICMP operate independently, that is, not accountable to, for example, law enforcement, police, those kinds of justice -- or those kinds of justice stakeholders?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes. ICMP is an independent institution not connected with law enforcement or prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Has the ICMP assisted in the work of the Tribunal, particularly the Office of the Prosecutor, with respect to the analysis of DNA material?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes. In the past we have provided information relating to our independent programme upon request from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And has the ICMP provided DNA material or reports, information, to other organisations or entities besides the ICTY or the OTP?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, we have co-operated with the Bosnian State Court and we have co-operative agreements also with other governments, the Cyprus missing persons committee. We do all the DNA testing with Cyprus missing persons presently. We have worked in the past very extensively with the UN Mission in Kosovo which has now been transferred to the EULEX mission there, and all these agencies we share the results of our DNA testing and matching.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You had mentioned a little bit earlier that one of the areas that you were responsible for had to do with anthropological and pathological analysis relative to exhumations and so on. Is this part of the Examinations and Excavations Division?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, it would be. I have to clarify that there has been an internal name change at the ICMP. What we used to call the Examinations and Excavations Division we now refer to as the Archaeology and Anthropology Division, but the functional role remains the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You also mentioned the Identification and Co-ordination Division as well as the laboratory system. How many laboratories does the ICMP operate currently?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: We operate two different laboratories that are involved in the DNA testing process. Both of these laboratories are involved in the testing of each and every sample of human remains that is submitted to the ICMP. The first laboratory is in Banja Luka, in the Republika Srpska, where part of the testing process occurs and the DNA testing is completed in our other DNA laboratory in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Doctor, you've mentioned that the two lab facilities and the Identification Co-ordination Division Support the Forensic Science Program as well as -- but let me ask you, does the ICMP also maintain mortuary facilities?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That situation has changed a bit over time, but fundamentally the answer to the question is yes. ICMP has either managed it directly or seconded anthropological experts to assist at mortuary facilities in numerous places in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the Podrinje Identification Project?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, that was a large mortuary facility essentially dedicated to the issue of Srebrenica that the ICMP established in co-operation with the court-appointed pathologist who worked in a dual role, both in direct co-operation and as an employee of the ICMP as well as serving an official function as a court-appointed pathologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is the Podrinje Identification Project, or the mortuary facility, still managed by or operated by the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No. Full responsibility for the conduct of that mortuary has now been turned over to state authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Does the ICMP or has the ICMP operated blood collection centres for the purposes of obtaining samples in order to conduct DNA analysis against bones that are recovered from various excavation sites?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, that is a primary role of the Identification Co-ordination Division, and through a number of very extensive activities, blood samples obtained as small droplets of blood on a particular type of preservative card have been sought and obtained from thousands of family members who are reporting missing persons to the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just so that we're clear for the record, can you tell us when the laboratory system at the ICMP became operational?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Near the end of 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what type of DNA testing is carried out by these facilities in the simplest of terms?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Our primary method that extends to virtually all the cases that are of interest to this Court is the same that is referred to as DNA finger-printing and is widely used in criminal casework worldwide, including criminal offender databases. And this is a form of nuclear DNA testing, probably the simplest way to refer to it is STR testing, short tandem repeat testing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How long has the ICMP employed this particular type of DNA testing?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Since the outset in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to the types of materials that the ICMP receives or analyses, is this type of testing consistent with the industry standard in DNA analysis?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: To your knowledge, are there better or more effective means of DNA testing or analysis that are available with respect to typing or matching skeletal remains or degraded skeletal remains, such as, for example, mitochondrial DNA analysis or PCR analysis?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, I will attempt to avoid a great deal of technical explanation. There are a number of different methods where variable DNA information can be obtained from degraded remains. One of them that has been widely used on highly degraded samples is mitochondrial DNA analysis or mtDNA analysis which is, in fact, more sensitive type of testing, meaning you have an increased chance of obtaining a DNA profile from mitochondrial DNA. That is simply because it's a multi-copy element, every cell has many copies; and therefore, it's less likely that all of the copies will have degraded. However, mitochondrial DNA is by no means a definitive identifier. You can and will match multiple individuals in the population, and so it has not proven an effective means of identification in the very large number of missing persons in the former Yugoslavia. The STR testing that we use widely is, on the other hand, extremely discriminating, capable of -- to any reasonable level of doubt identifying an individual with certainty as a single individual, and moreover making that certain match through comparisons to family relatives of the missing person. I would like to add one further clarification with regard to your question. You mentioned PCR testing. Both STR analysis and the mitochondrial DNA analysis involve the process of PCR, which stands for the polymerase chain reaction. It is a bedrock technique of amplifying selected target regions of DNA from very, very small amounts of DNA that was originally recovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you 65 ter 5921. Do you recognise what's on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't want to -- I'm not going to go into your report in any depth, but does it describe, generally speaking, the manner in which DNA analyses were conducted by the ICMP throughout the period that's indicated here, 2001 to 2008?

utterances.text: Yes. A DNA scientist could review that quickly and have a good understanding of the basic methodology used in our laboratory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you mentioned a few minutes ago -- or you referred to the standard operating procedures. If you could, please tell the Trial Chamber what the role of these standard operating procedures are with respect to the DNA testing that's carried out by ICMP. Are these guide-lines? Are these rules? Are these regulations? Just so that they have an idea of what you're talking about in your report.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, I think a useful, everyday analogy would be that this is a cookbook for how one performs DNA analysis. So it's a highly specified set of instructions that the trained analysts follow. The concept of a standard operating procedure is anchored in ICMP's comprehensive quality management system, where our techniques are very carefully validated through control experiments and documented; and then the staff members engaged in those testing procedures are formally trained and checked off in those techniques and have periodic annual competency tests where their work is scrutinised and evaluated. And then they are deemed competent to continue with that activity. All of these steps relate to ICMP's internationally recognised accreditation to the ISO 17025 guide-line rules for laboratory science, and this is an accreditation that is awarded to us through the German national accreditation agency that has the acronym DAkkS.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When was the ICMP awarded this particular accreditation, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The two different components were -- of the DNA identification process were awarded their accreditation at different times. The DNA laboratory system was accredited in late 2007 and, if I'm remembering correctly, shortly afterwards, in 2008, the Identification Co-ordination Division achieved its accreditation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is the accrediting agency -- rather, does the accrediting agency play a role in determining the standard operating procedures that are implemented or adopted by the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Actually, no. They do not specify the methods that we have to use. They do specify the documentation that regulates the conduct of our testing and they do inspect our experimental validation reports that demonstrate the validity of our techniques.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And prior to the accreditation that you received in 2007 -- or rather, following the accreditation, has there been any substantial change between how the ICMP conducted DNA analysis before accreditation and after its accreditation in 2007? Were new procedures adopted? Were new protocols followed? That sort of thing. If you can just tell us generally.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, generally, the field of forensic DNA analysis continues to develop, and given the expertise of our staff and the novel and high-throughput challenges we face, very often the ICMP is working at the forefront of developing and optimising techniques. Simply put, we're essentially the best in the world at this because of our extreme experience working with this material. So with that said, there's a continual evolution of the protocols that we use, updates to software, new models of instrumentation, various implementation of quality-control mechanisms that decrease the already low chance for some type of human error. So yes, there have been changes continually, and that includes since our accreditation and since the methodology report that you showed earlier. I would like to emphasise, though, that there was no fundamental shift in methodology pre- and post-accreditation. We performed basically the same type of DNA testing to essentially the same standards before and after accreditation.

utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Doctor, I wanted to ask you just a few questions about the process by which matches are made and match process is undertaken, and I know that you've described a lot of this in your report. But just in very simple terms, what is matched against what?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, as previously described, we obtain STR DNA profiles from human remains recovered primarily from mass graves but from many other contexts as well, and we also obtain STR DNA profiles from family members of the missing. So family members come forward, report a missing person, and then we obtain reference samples from those individuals, transform that into DNA profiles and upload that into a very large database. Then every time we get a DNA profile from a skeletal sample, for example, we run that profile against the entire DNA database representing all the family members, and using genetic similarity indices are able to pick out the families that match and then in the end perform a formal calculation that arrives at a statistic indicating the certainty of association. And the ICMP will issue a DNA match report when that certainty reaches a minimum threshold value of 99.95 per cent. However, I would like to emphasise that a vast majority of our DNA matches have a great deal higher certainty than that. Sometimes 99 point and then following that would be 12 nines or eighteen 9s. So very, very, very certain matches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, could I ask the following to you, Mr. Parsons. STR, do I understand it well that you take various points on the DNA material and then the more you take, the higher the probability, if there's a full match, like with finger-prints there you need a minimum, I think, of 12 points of comparison which would have to match and of course no point of a non-match. Is that how I have to understand the STR because you can't do the whole of the DNA but you just take how many? Is that 13 or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In our current system it's 15 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- and plus a different locus that tells you what sex the individual was. So your explanation was very much on target. I would just want to add that each of these 15 separate loci is independent of the other ones and each of those loci can vary in the populations. So you have two copies of your DNA, one from your mother and one from your father, and there's one location on that DNA that we would test. And you can have any of a number of variants on either of the maternal or paternal copy. So you may have a random match at one locus with somebody else in the population of, say, 1 in 100. But at the second locus that's also 1 in 100, so now you can see that it goes up very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you say unrelated, for example, if I would compare that, I do know that it's not about the visible features, but the one would be the colour of the eyes and the other thing would be something totally different. That is that the unrelated -- let's just assume that those are unrelated --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could I show you 65 ter 25704. It should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'll refrain from mentioning any names in this document, but do you recognise what it is, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: This would be a DNA match report issued by the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There's just a couple of things I'd like to go over with you. We can see some numbers here. First we see the identity and the degree of familiar -- familial relationship with the person to be identified. It's a wife, a son, mother indicated. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes. The indication of wife, son, and mother are three people who gave blood samples and who we have typed and now compared to this missing individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And it indicates here that the DNA results obtained from the bone sample are 3.84e12 times more likely if the bone sample originated from an individual related to the blood references in a manner as described on this report than to another unrelated individual in the general population. Is this -- first of all, could you tell us what that number is, 3.84e12? What does it stand for?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, very first of all that's simply a scientific notation that is shorthand for that number should be 384 followed by 12 zeros -- or excuse me, 10 zeros. And that actually represents a -- the primary statistical outcome of the DNA test and that number is the likelihood ratio. It's not listed here on the report, but I'll just put it out there because it's actually, I think, a fairly easy concept to grasp. What this means is that we can now be 3.84 times 10 to the 12th times more certain that it is this individual than we were prior to doing the DNA test. So in Bayesian statistics, the likelihood ratio is the factor by which you "update" your uncertainty. You had a certain amount of uncertainty to begin with, and now we're 3.84 trillion times more sure than we were before about that particular hypothesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There's an indicate -- I'm sorry, let me just pause for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I abuse that in posing one additional question. The wife is not biologically related to the missing person, whereas his mother and his son are. Is that to allow you to make a comparison with the other family members and especially the son or is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Especially the son --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- that's right. The son would be made up half of the missing person and half of the mother, so having her information adds greatly to the certainty of the match.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And this is purely the biological element of all of this, I mean the fact that the missing person, at least whether there's suspicion that this might be the DNA of a missing person, of course there's other factors such as where he lived, that he disappeared, et cetera, are adding to the probability but then in a non-biological way. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in a non-biological and also generally non-numerical way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Also, we can see another statistic at the very bottom of this document -- well, in this same paragraph in the middle of the page, rather, and it says -- and it refers to the probability of relatedness, as you indicated previously, 99.99999 per cent when using prior odds of 1 in 7.000. Can you explain just very briefly to the Chamber what these prior odds mean?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes. The prior odds relate to what I said before about the concept of updating uncertainty. So not considering any evidence apart from the DNA evidence and where this bone sample came from regionally, we have a prior probability, that is, before you do the DNA test, of 1 in 7.000. Let me explain what that means. Let's say I go to a Srebrenica-related grave in this region and pick up a bone and you ask me: What are the chances that it's one of these 7.000 people reported missing, a specific one of these 7.000 people reported missing from Srebrenica? And I would say: 1 in 7.000. I have no additional information. So that's my prior probability. That's what the chances are that this is going to be any single named individual. I then do the DNA test and we update that uncertainty by the likelihood ratio, which is that 3.84 times 10 to the 12th and now we are so much more sure, we started at 1 chance in 7.000 and now we're at greater than 99.99999 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for your explanation.

But do the differences in the prior odds substantially affect the surety level that's indicated in the match report?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: For purposes of clarity, let me again repeat that we use different prior probabilities based on the number of individuals missing from a particular region or event that we know this sample -- that we judge this sample to be relating to. So here we have 1 in 4.500 from a different region of Bosnia, versus 1 in 7.000. The answer is: Does it affect the outcome of the calculations? It does by exactly the ratio of 7.000 to 4.500, in other words, less than a factor of 2, which is not very significant compared to ten orders of magnitude or 12 orders of magnitude, that is to say, 12 zeros after the number to begin with. So minor changes in the prior probability do almost nothing to affect the surety of these DNA match reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In this particular document, in the paragraph that's just above the stamp, it indicates that there is an inconsistency on loci, it says Penta E between the alleged son and father. And it says: "Appears to represent a mutational event." Can you just acquaint us very briefly with what that means in terms of either the surety of the identification or the reliability of the identification?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, this thing that is referred to as a mutational event is a rare occurrence but it's very well-known to happen in this type of testing, and the ICMP in the very high volume of work we do encounters it with some regularity. And we take one step backward with respect to biology. If you remember, I said that these STR loci are highly variable. That's why they're good for distinguishing one individual from the next. The way that variability becomes established in the population is, in fact, through mutation. One person has one thing and then one of his offspring has something different. That's a genetic mutation. And because these STR loci mutate quickly, sometimes you see them in actual casework. So we have an instance here where going from the father to the son we would have to invoke a mutation. We would have to assume or conclude that a mutation has occurred in order for that to actually be the father of that son. We here have a large number of family references, so it's quite clear that he, in fact, is, but that there was a mutation. We know the frequency with which these mutations occur so we actually are able to put that in the calculation and adjust our overall level of certainty that takes into account all the matching with all the family members and, additionally, the fact that there was a fairly rare event that had to happen that actually makes it less certainty than it would have been without the mutation. But taken in total, it's still as certain as is listed on this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one question, you are referring to the compared materials as from the son or -- now that may not be the biological son of the person who is registered as the father. How do you deal with that? What's your conclusion then, that it's not that person or that -- I mean, you can draw various conclusions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, we're comparing basically two different hypotheses. It is or it is not -- there is or there is not the stated biological relationship. This number that is being reported here is the conclusion that it is, in fact, the biological relationship and that that is the father, even though there had to have been a mutation. We're able to take into account the fact that these mutations occur rarely, so we're surprised to see it and therefore our certainty diminishes. But taken in total with all the evidence, we still are able to conclude with this level of certainty that that is the missing person in question and that that is his father.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the categories at the top of this table is ICMP 1, ICMP 2, ICMP 3, et cetera. Are these the loci which you have used? Because you said you'd used 15, whereas I find 16 there?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.text: It does have a bearing because had a DNA profile not been obtained, it would be impossible to match it. However, it is also possible to obtain a DNA profile from a bone sample but not to find a match to the family reference database.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In this particular case, as we have a named individual, that would indicate that there exists a match report for the DNA profile with respect to the blood donors or the people indicated in the database?

utterances.text: Well, if there's no significant difference between the three -- of course, the Defence has an opportunity to compare and ask further questions. utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I note from the page here that this sample was submitted from a pathologist by the name of Dr. Vedo Tuco, and he would have been the individual responsible for forwarding that sample to the ICMP. The ICMP would take only one of those bone samples that they deem the most suitable or -- that is to say, the most likely to give a DNA result and that is what would have been reported. utterances.text: You would choose at what stage, when taking a sample or any sample sent to you, received by you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Finally, therefore, the conclusion is that one of these bones matches with --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: This is a spreadsheet that the ICMP provided to the OTP and the Trial Chamber depicting all the DNA match reports that the ICMP has developed that we consider related to the 1995 fall of Srebrenica up until January 31st, 2013.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you just a few questions about how it's formatted. What I'd like to do is just go through a couple of the categories on the top here. We can see first obviously names, date of birth, then we see protocol ID. Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The protocol number is a number that the ICMP assigns when a DNA match between a bone sample and a family is found, and it simply refers to the report itself. So it's a sequential designator of a DNA match report associated with a particular individual. If we look at the format we see 9 -- on the very top one in row 2, under protocol ID we see the number 9662/07 and that would be the 9.662nd DNA match report in the year 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Next to that we see a case ID, and can you tell us -- let's stick with row number 2. Can you tell us what that denotes?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That is the sample identifier. So a bone sample has been submitted to the ICMP through any number of means and that is the name that we have that designates what that sample is. The ICMP normally does not have control of the naming convention, although we do have recommended guide-lines to follow, and this one appears to have followed those recommendations where this comes from the Kamenica or Cancari Road grave 10, and then other components of this are related to either the site or the skeletal element that has been sampled. LF here should designate a left femur. But in terms of what the ICMP does with the sample, we don't care what its name is except to use that to keep track of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are there mechanisms in place to address expectation or outcome expectations with respect to samples that are received from the mortuary for testing?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, that goes to one of the primary strengths of DNA evidence and DNA testing is the potential for objectivity in the outcome. So the analysts are not making subjective experience-based decisions for the most part. And what the ICMP does to maximise that objectivity is to, in fact, strip that case ID number from the sample all together before it is submitted to the DNA laboratory. And this is a function of the Identification Co-ordination Division. Instead of that case ID number, we assign it a unique but randomly generated bar code and that is how the sample transitions its way through the DNA laboratory process. At the end of that DNA process, a profile is generated, but as far as the DNA staff know, it is only associated with some random number and no information about what grave it came from, what event it came from, what region it came from, and certainly what family it may be associated with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, is that for purposes of potential bias, that if you have that information that you might be inclined to link it to the most likely family member that would be available and that therefore you make it more or less anonymous only with a -- that random number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It addresses bias really at two levels. One is that -- at the level of investigator inspection, where if the analyst knows a pre-existing hypothesis, sometimes his mental processes will superimpose on that to result in bias. So yes, it's designed to eliminate that. But then secondly, there's also the social concept of political bias that we encounter in the former Yugoslavia and this is designed to be able to also say: We have no idea what "side" this sample comes from, what ethnic origin this sample comes from, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and therefore no one would be inclined either to positively identify a Serb, a Croat, or a Muslim, and you avoid that by this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us very quickly what is the ID ICMP? That's indicated here in column E?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: We saw that before on a DNA match report. The ICMP ID number is the number that's assigned to the missing person rather than to the bone sample. And so you will have an ICMP ID number whether or not you've been identified as a missing person, and this simply indicates that this is, in that row, the 8.558th person to register their family member missing in our system.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Next we have the site name and here it's indicated Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could scroll over to the right of the spreadsheet a little bit further we can probably accommodate a few more rows.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We see the site co-ordinates and then it says "jurisdiction," in this case BiH Federal Commission. Can you just explain very quickly what that is?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That's the agency under whose authority the grave was excavated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We can see here the date of submission. Is that the date that the report is submitted or the date that the sample is submitted for testing?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And meaning the match report?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the date of disappearance, we can see here in this row, 11.7.1995. Can you explain what this nominal value is?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: When we obtain a report -- when families come to the ICMP to report a missing person, we very carefully document a number of lines of information about that missing person. First of all, clearly document his name, clearly document his relationship to the person reporting him missing, clearly document his relationship to other individuals, other family members who would prevent -- provide a DNA sample. And we also obtain information about the place and date of disappearance of the individual, where last seen. You made reference to the word -- you used the word "nominal," and normally that is not a nominal category, but in the case of the July 1995 fall of Srebrenica we adopted a convention of designating the date for events related to that general scenario as the 11th of July, 1995. And the reason we did that is that there are thousands of family members that we have dealt with to get samples, well over 10.000. I think it's about -- I think it's over 12.000 family members from whom we've received DNA samples. And each one of those donors is interviewed separately. And we have the chaos of a refugee population in and around Srebrenica, the rapidly unfolding chaotic events, and so you'll ask one family member, "When was he last seen?" And they might say, "I last saw him on the 9th of July when we were separated." Meanwhile, another family member may have accompanied the man into the forest to try and go over land and say, "I last saw him on the 11th of July." So because there were so many minorly conflicting lines of evidence here and because the amount of work was so large in registering all these people, the ICMP identification staff adopted the convention of: We'll put the date of the 11th of July as associated with this particular event.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me just ask very quickly because I want to filter this spreadsheet so that I can take you -- draw your attention to another area. But here we have an indication of forest -- place of disappearance, forest, Potocari. And then we have a column indicating a main case of association. Can you tell the Chamber with respect to place of disappearance what that denotes and why and also with respect to what a main case is versus a reassociation so that the Chamber is clear on that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: With regard to place of disappearance, again different family members were very likely to provide slightly different information about where the person was last seen, and those in the end mapped on to two primary groups of individuals. One reflects the group of men and boys who attempted to flee Srebrenica in the days just ahead of July 11th in a large column that tried to break out over land and those were designated as forest, the person tried to make his way through the forest. And then the other designation is Potocari, and that would reflect individuals who did not join the column of men but who instead stayed behind in Srebrenica and wound up at the DutchBat base in Potocari and then were subsequently separated from the women and eventually executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the main case versus a reassociation. Can you tell us just very briefly what that is?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, one hallmark characteristic of the forensic investigation of Srebrenica graves that has not yet been referred to is the issue of secondary graves. So we have the circumstance where thousands of individuals were buried in the first instance in July of 1995 in very large primary mass graves, so basically their entire body was deposited in huge mass graves. Subsequent to that, after the passage of a number of months, those graves were exhumed by heavy equipment by the perpetrators and put into trucks and taken about the country-side in Eastern Bosnia and deposited then in a large series of secondary mass graves. We have in fact 39 large secondary mass graves that are associated with five extremely large primary mass graves and execution events. A consequence of this heavy equipment exhumation of the bodies months after they were initially buried caused those bodies to disintegrate, fall apart, and become jumbled together, so that we're dealing in many instances not with bodies but with disarticulated body parts and that is where we get the main case versus a reassociation case. So, for example, the anthropologist will look at a case which may be only the lower half of a body, take a sample from the femur and send it to the ICMP. This is coming from a particular grave-site. The ICMP develops a DNA profile, matches it against the database, and identifies the individual to whom that sample refers. It will have been the first time we have seen this individual and that will be called a main case. It was the first instance of a DNA match to that individual. Months later or years later or what have you, a secondary mass grave may be -- an additional secondary mass grave may be excavated and they'll find the upper portion of that same individual, we'll get a DNA match there, and we'll issue it as the same protocol number but as a reassociation case rather than a main case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'd like to do is to filter this list for the Cerska grave-site and I'd like to ask you just a couple of questions about that.

utterances.text: Yes. First of all, I'd like to emphasise the word "or" in that -- in those two names. So we have a DNA profile from a single individual and in this case we can't distinguish which of two brothers this individual is, and that is a characteristic of DNA testing when you have, for example, only the parents as reference samples. You can know for sure that this individual is the son of these two parents, but you can't determine which of two missing siblings this might be. The person's name is simply not written on DNA. So we can define exactly what the relationship is, we can know that these two individuals are brothers to each other, we can know that they're both sons of the same parents, but we can't distinguish one from another by DNA. We know we have at least -- we know we have one or the other of them. We issue the DNA match report in the name of both.

One of them is reported missing from Srebrenica, the other one from a previous era, say 1992. And remember I described earlier conditions under which DNA cannot distinguish between one sibling and the other. So this would be an instance where we simply had a DNA match to one or the other of these siblings and then later on found out through the identification process that another individual had been matched as the brother associated with Srebrenica so we took the other brother off the list after that finding became apparent to us.

utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll need back up in e-court -- oh, in Sanction, the spreadsheet we were just looking at.
