utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, you have until 12.40.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I was about to ask you, Dr. Parsons, about the explanation concerning the inconclusively associated cases, if we could just go to that tab. And here we can see that there are a number of cases and we can go over to the right-hand side so we can look at some of these explanations, but can you explain, maybe in general terms since it is pretty well explicated here, what the reason for this category is.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes. Very briefly, either the evidence is contradictory or mixed regarding whether it should be considered as related to the fall of Srebrenica or not. Here we -- one instance would be different information from different members of the family because we did have that -- that disagreement, we weren't comfortable putting it in the first very large list. Here we have -- I'll make an example, also from row 8, where it says: "Person killed before the fall of Srebrenica remains known to be buried at the hospital location in Srebrenica," so I -- we would leave it to any observer to conclude whether that is associated or not. That's why it's not in the original list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the information -- sorry, let me just take a pause for a second. The information that you received in relation to determining whether or not a case was inconclusively associated or excluded as associated from the large list of match reports concerning Srebrenica, is that information derived from external sources?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The primary source of that information comes from the families themselves that report the person missing, but we do take into consideration really kind of all that we know about it. So in some of the excluded cases, they were excluded primarily because they came from grave-sites that would be inconsistent with being missing from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you another spreadsheet, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, I'd like to tender this document first. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 29076 receives number P1727, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1727 is admitted into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I'd like to show the witness 65 ter 29078.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you see that in the screen in front of you, Dr. Parsons?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's entitled: "Srebrenica unmatched DNA profiles to June 7th 2013," and then it refers to reassociation profiles list. Can you just tell us as succinctly and briefly as possible what this list shows?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, we previously were looking at a very large list of individuals that had been identified through DNA matching from profiles from the graves. Here is a list in -- shown in two columns of DNA profiles that were obtained from graves considered to be related to Srebrenica, both by ICMP and the ICTY, but they have not been matched to family members, presumably and almost certainly because we do not have family reference samples for them to match. So these are unidentified DNA profiles that clearly indicate the presence of a new and unique individual. We just don't know who it was, but he came from one of the Srebrenica-associated graves. And then we have in the left-most column, the designations in blue, those are the unique individuals. And then to the right, associated with that are additional body parts that match the first person. So we see in rows 3 and 4, just for example, both the blue and the red profile come from the same individual. So that unknown individual is then found in two parts. Then we go down to the next set of three rows, 5 through 7, and we have three different parts of the same individual, again unmatched as to family member but representing a unique individual associated with Srebrenica. And there are 124 unmatched individuals represented in that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much for that explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, I'd like to tender this exhibit as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 29078 receives number P1728, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1728 is admitted into evidence. There are no names on it, no need to have it under seal, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President, no need to have it under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This will be a public document. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to this list of unmatched DNA profiles and the larger list of matched DNA profiles, is it fair to say that each profile of a main case refers to an individual?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. So we would have -- in terms of the total number of individuals from the first list, I think we said 67 -- 6.708, I can also report the current value because that list is as of January. As of early June there were 6.767 individuals identified by name in addition to the 124 unidentified here, for a total of 7.001 individuals, distinct individuals, known by DNA to have been recovered from these graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Right. Thank you very much for that explanation in the update. Just one last question, and that is: In your opinion, is the DNA identification matching process that's been undertaken by the ICMP and currently undertaken by the ICMP reliable to a high degree of scientific certainty?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions of the witness at this time. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Mr. Stojanovic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, good afternoon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Parsons, you'll be cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Understood. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will try, Professor, to go very briefly over certain topics that remain after the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to call up in e-court P1723. This is a document under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What I wanted to ask, Professor, you said in response from the Chamber that from the photograph that we see the mortal remains were provided to you by the pathologist and you take samples for DNA profiling from the appropriate parts. It is said here that this was done by Dr. Vedo Tuco. Is he an employee of the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is he an employee of the Podrinje Identification Centre?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How is he involved in this entire process as a provider of this kind of information for your analysis?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: He is one of the state court-appointed pathologists that is authorised to perform autopsies, issue death certificates, and in that responsibility submits samples also to the ICMP. He works in Tuzla at a -- at the commemorative centre there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You do not oversee his work? I suppose you have no way to supervise him?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Also, you in the ICMP are not concerned with the issue whether the mortal remains that were photographed were really the mortal remains of one body. It is Dr. Vedo Tuco who does that, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: In this particular case, I would answer in the affirmative. But in general, we are concerned with that issue and our anthropologists are involved in a great number of these cases and, in fact, may have assisted Dr. Tuco on many occasions to make that -- to make that determination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And another question that follows from the examination-in-chief. In the status of the Podrinje Identification Centre, who is the founder of that centre?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: ICMP established that centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does the centre in Tuzla have a laboratory that is also used for DNA matching?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No. All the DNA work is done by the ICMP, not at PIP, Podrinje Identification Project.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a man who worked for the ICMP and is now working at the Podrinje Identification Project. What kind of profile of specialist is he?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: He is also a court-appointed forensic pathologist who has managed the Podrinje Identification Project throughout the entirety of its existence and he's a highly experienced forensic pathologist who conducts autopsies and has extreme familiarity with osteology and physical anthropology as well. His name is Dr. Rifat Kesetovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from Dr. Rifat Kesetovic we have seen in these reports another name, namely Dr. Zdenko Cihlarz. Am I right, and if so, what is his status in the entire process?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That is correct and he is also a court-appointed pathologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you assist me on this, Professor. When you spoke about the organisation that verifies the work of laboratories like yours, I have before me data obtained from an organisation whose acronym is GEDNAP, a German organisation. Is that the same one that we talked about when you used the acronym DAkkS?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No, that's a completely different organisation. The GEDNAP group is involved in providing proficiency tests where they send samples to different laboratories, and these samples have known and expected results. And it's part of the quality control exercises of a laboratory to conduct testing on those and see if they get the same result as GEDNAP. So GEDNAP is not actually an accreditation body of any kind. They simply provide these known samples and report on the results. I will say, though, that ICMP also participates in GEDNAP proficiency testing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is GEDNAP a body who can also issue ICMP with a certificate for the work of laboratories?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I heard the witness say a minute ago: "So GEDNAP is not actually an accreditation body of any kind ..." Which seems to answer your question. Unless I misunderstood you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You understood correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then I did not understand this quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You obtained accreditation in 2007, as you said. Now, before 2007, were you involved in DNA matching?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, since 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: From 2001 until 2007, ICMP did not have accreditation for the work of its laboratories; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, how many DNA matches were done by your organisation between 2001 and 2007 before receiving accreditation?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No, but the answer would be quite many -- because I simply do not recall that exact number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are we talking in the hundreds? Are we talking in the thousands? Could you give us a rough estimate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Definitely talking in the thousands. As you -- you saw that list for Srebrenica alone was 16.000 match reports. So, yeah, very many reports were issued prior to 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we're even talking close to the tens of thousands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you kindly tell us how many verified accredited laboratories does ICMP now have in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, our DNA laboratory system and our Identification Co-ordination Division are both accredited. The DNA laboratory system is involved in two facilities, one in Banja Luka and one in Sarajevo, and the Identification Co-ordination Division is in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put one additional question to you, Dr. Parsons. When was this accreditation system established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not quite sure, but I would beg leave of the Court to comment on that general topic insofar as the issue of forensic laboratory accreditation in the field of forensic DNA testing has been quite evolutionary. At the time that the ICMP began in 2001, very, very few labs worldwide were accredited to the ISO standard. As the field progressed, there was more and more laboratories thinking about doing that. I was a member of the European Network of Forensic Science Institutes in 2006 and 2007, while the ICMP was making the determination if we should go after accreditation. And the European Network of Forensic Science Institutes did a trans-Europe survey of criminalistic forensic DNA laboratories to determine how many were accredited, and at that time it was less than 30 per cent of all practicing forensic laboratories. However, to put the evolution in context, at that time fully 50 per cent of the ones that were not accredited were also in preparation for applying for accreditation, which can take years. And it was at that time that the ICMP decided that we ought to also, now that this was -- this accreditation movement was becoming more de rigueur for quality management systems, we decided to go for it ourselves. So there is no great change in the quality of ICMP's work pre-and post-accreditation, nor were we in any way exceptional with working without accreditation at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the context of the same question, could we please look at 1D1110.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And we need to look at paragraph 1 on page 3, Professor. And before that, just glance at the cover page because it's about GEDNAP. Thank you. Now let us move to page 3, paragraph 1. I highlighted the passage that I want to ask you about. It says here that the system to which you will belong, and I quote: "... must comply with the generally accepted state-of-the-art which means that the system must not only be proven to be reproducible within the developing laboratory but must also be reproducible in other equally qualified laboratories." I ask you now: Would you accept that a scientifically valid principle is reproducibility in other equally qualified laboratories?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Can you clarify for me, please, what this document is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to ask you an additional question, Mr. Stojanovic. You're talking about the system. Now, on the previous page I read that it is about basic principles of the blind trial system, that is apparently the system adopted by GEDNAP to -- Mr. Mladic, low volume. So the witness asked to know what the document is, and my question is: When you refer to the system, page 3, to be clear on what system that refers to. And if I could read the title of the document, it is the: "GEDNAP German DNA Profiling Group Blind Trial System," and it exists of 16 pages which, as far as the index on the first page is concerned, seems to describe the system GEDNAP is using for its activities. Anything to add, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. And if I may, maybe that should have been the first step, we could look at page 2, introductory remarks, that perhaps provide the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, as a matter of fact, I would suggest that you look first at page 1 where there is an index of what follows. And then perhaps slowly move it so that the witness can gain an impression of what the document is about. If you're ready to move below 3.1, please indicate so that you can see the following.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we move. Yes. Mr. Stojanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I think I'm going to ask you again. From the passage that I've read out to you, would you accept that the reproducibility of results from one laboratory to another as the scientifically valid principle.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: As a very general answer to your question, I would say that demonstration of reproducibility is one element of an overarching quality management system that should be taken very seriously and implemented to the extent possible. In fact, the existence of the GEDNAP blind trial is to permit participating laboratories with an opportunity to test results -- to test samples that have already been tested in qualified laboratories. Therefore, by participating in the GEDNAP trial, they are offering a means by which to comply with this element of a quality management system and that's the very rationale for the reason that we participate in the GEDNAP programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any other laboratory that checked the results you obtained by matching the samples that you've discussed today?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: In the Hurricane Katrina disaster in the United States with the -- for the state of Louisiana, we provided DNA testing on all the victim samples that were done in that incident response. The United States authorities decided to have two laboratories independently test all of those samples, and so we were involved in a very large real-life disaster and degraded DNA testing project where there was full duplication of results. We got exactly the same results as the other internationally recognised laboratory that was involved in this process, with the exception of one result, where very energetic investigation proved that the ICMP result was the correct one and that the other laboratory had made an error.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, do you have such reports of the verification by other laboratories in terms of their results that you have obtained? Are they available for the scientific community to view as well as for our team in this case?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: The Hurricane Katrina undertaking I just referred to was in no means a quality-control exercise, so, no, we would not have such a document. However, the GEDNAP blind trials that we participate in do have a letter acknowledging the results of the trial, so those would be available.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you mentioned the laboratories in Sarajevo and Banja Luka, up to what level on -- of work in the overall process is the Banja Luka laboratory involved forwarding their results to be continued in terms of the work to be performed by the laboratory in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: That has changed over time. In the early years, the Banja Luka laboratory was involved in full DNA testing independently. In the last -- since just about 2006, however, in the interests of uniform mechanisms, uniform quality-control procedures, and cost and time efficiency, we changed so that there was a single operating procedure for all samples, and the work conducted by the Banja Luka laboratory now is constrained to the bone sample cleaning, the bone sample decontamination, and the bone sample grinding prior to chemical extraction, and that is a very specialised set of physical and chemical manipulations that makes a lot of sense to have in a dedicated facility. So they do the steps I just referred to on every bone sample as a specialised facility and then send them on for further processing on to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the overall process at any point in time, are the services of the Banja Luka laboratory relied on?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I just indicated what the Banja Luka laboratory does for each and every sample.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I see whether there may be some confusion there. You explained the change in the system since 2006. It may be that Mr. Stojanovic would also like to know whether you would rely on other activities done by the Banja Luka laboratory before 2006.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That -- if that's the case, that does clarify. Thank you. And the answer is: Yes, there are profiles in our DNA matching database that were derived wholly in the Banja Luka laboratory prior to that switch in procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will repeat my question, as I believe there was a problem in terminology. My question was: In the overall process at any point in time, are the services of the Tuzla laboratory relied on?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to Tuzla, that has also been an evolutionary process. The Identification Co-ordination Division is housed in Tuzla now and is not involved in the DNA testing procedure. They are an accessioning and matching specialised function. However, in the early years of the ICMP, the Tuzla centre had a DNA laboratory that was involved in conducting bone profile DNA testing. So -- and, excuse me, I apologise, a correction is they were involved in testing the blood samples that came from the family references.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That is why I wanted to ask you the following. Before 2006 and after 2006, did they conduct analysis of blood samples in their laboratory that are to be relied on for the purposes of matching to obtain identification?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: "They" meaning the Tuzla laboratory? The answer is yes, but when I say "relied upon," I don't mean blindly relied upon. For every DNA match that is issued, there is a full technical review of the data. So we don't blindly use the profile that comes from the Tuzla laboratory; we independently analyse the genetic electropherograms to make sure that they comport with current-day, quality-control standards. And if there is any question about anything, whether it comes from the Tuzla laboratory or anywhere else, those samples will be promptly retested in the Sarajevo DNA laboratory. I would like to emphasise that testing from blood samples is comparatively very routine compared to the much more difficult work that we do on bone samples. So it's a trivial undertaking to repeat that test if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you to explain the word "genetic electropherograms."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm just collecting my thoughts to try to give a useful but not too technical answer. The DNA profiles are obtained by selectively recovering or amplifying - you can use the two words interchangeably - small fragments of DNA that differ in size. These STR loci are variable insofar as they have variable lengths. And in order to determine that length, the fragments of DNA that have been recovered are put on a laser machine and separated by size, and that process is known as electrophoresis. The DNA molecules migrate through a matrix that separates them by size, the laser causes them to be detected. And so when I referred to the genetic electropherograms, what I mean is the output of the instrument that allows you to detect peaks that correspond to fragments of particular lengths and then you can easily translate that into the genetic profile in question. I hope there was some clarity to that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps I may not have understood the full hundred per cent, but at least it gave me an impression. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic. You may have understood the full hundred per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Only partially, Your Honour. There is a lot to be learned on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, was the Tuzla laboratory certified and accredited at any point in time to conduct that work?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: No, that was prior to any decision to seek accreditation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would I be correct if I said the Tuzla laboratory to date has no necessary certification, at least not in the sense of what you have for Banja Luka and Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I -- before the witness answers the question, could you, Mr. Stojanovic, explain what you mean by "necessary certification," because I understood from the answers of the witness that the certification system is on the basis -- is on a voluntary basis, although developing strongly among the -- in the field of where these laboratories are working. What do you mean by "necessary" --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you're completely correct. I do not see it as obligatory. However, having in mind what the professor said, which is that scientific verification also included the use of the necessary standards needed to obtain verification, in that regard I wanted to ask whether the Tuzla lab has such certificate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please answer the question, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I realise it's a little bit difficult to follow the entire process, but let's -- I think we can simplify greatly by the following explanation: There is presently, and has not been for many years, a DNA laboratory in Tuzla that is affiliated with the ICMP. I referred earlier to some blood DNA profiling that was done by the Tuzla laboratory, but I think it was in 2004 - I apologise, I could be misremembering - that that laboratory was not sustained anymore at all. The ICMP does have a facility in Tuzla. It is not a DNA laboratory. It is where the Identification Co-ordination Division is housed, and that is the sample collection, sample accessioning, and DNA matching facility. There is no DNA laboratory. It's all computers. But that ICD, Identification Co-ordination Division, facility in Tuzla is fully accredited by our ISO 17025 process, the same as the laboratory system. So from the beginning of the DNA extraction to the match report at the end, involving processes both within the laboratories and in the Identification Co-ordination Division, that process is fully accredited since 2000 -- early 2008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one additional question. Are the samples preserved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All the samples, both from the -- taken from the remains found in the graves and of the family members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The family members, certainly. The samples from the grave it is a bit variable. Sometimes we will consume the entire sample. So the way it normally works - I don't think you got a good view of it - is that a body-bag will come in from the field where it has been exhumed from a grave. ICMP anthropologists and archaeologists will do a very good job of making sure to the best as they are able to do in the field of removing a part that is only part of a single individual. It may not be a complete body because it is not even there, but the idea is not to mix it together with other body parts. There are limitations on how accurately you can do that in the field. If it's done inexpertly, you can make a huge mess of a bad problem. But what happens is anthropologists in the mortuary facility will open the bag, take the remains out, wash them, very carefully scrutinise them, and determine whether there's a single individual represented or multiple individuals represented. Then in order to answer whatever questions they have in mind about co-mingling and fragmentation and as well as get an identification, they'll cut a small sample of bone, and that is what was sent to the DNA lab typically. We almost never see what was shown in that photograph with multiple bone samples. Then depending on the size of that sample and what was available for the anthropologist to take, we may or may not use all of that. Normally we would have enough left over for a reserve and we would save that but sometimes we use the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us an indication approximately in how many cases what percentage you would have used all the material and therefore the material not remaining available for a new test?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My intention in putting this estimate forward is to be as helpful as possible, while I really have to say it's going to be very rough, but I would say we probably retain material in 75 per cent of the time at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance. I will conclude with this topic. Professor, you mentioned a European Network of Forensic Science Institutes. I wanted to ask you this: Does the ICMP maintain any kind of professional relationship with this European network?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes, we do, actually in a rather unique manner. Formally constituted that European network involves police laboratories, but because we're kind of a unique organisation with regard to our mandate but also because of our prominence in the field, I was invited to be a regular contributing guest member. So ICMP has kind of a special status with ENFSI, that's the acronym, E-N-F-S-I. And we regularly attend the meetings, we're regularly asked to provide updates, and in fact we perform training programmes under the auspices of ENFSI. We have a number of instances where we have put on multi-day training programmes for forensic sciences scientists around Europe to come in and learn the specialised and difficult techniques that we do. We also assisted the Montenegrin police in developing techniques for bone DNA extraction through co-ordination with ENFSI.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you, the ICMP, a member of the ENFSI network?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness has told that he participated as a guest member. Mr. Stojanovic, it's always good to listen to the answers and not only to the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understood the Professor say that he participated in the work, but what I wanted to know whether the ICMP is a member of the professional organisation, as the organisation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we are not one of the police laboratories that is capable of being a member of ENFSI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness earlier referred to the special status, Mr. Stojanovic, which I would not use as an expression for ordinary membership. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honour, perhaps it is a good time to tender the document we relied on, which is 1D1110.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, no objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document receives number D326, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D326 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I checked with my colleagues, Mr. Stojanovic, but where you said you relied upon it, you were relying on a totally different exercise. You asked the witness questions about it, where it's -- as far as we are aware of, a proficiency developing system is something quite different from the testing of DNA material in the field. But since the parties apparently agree on relevance, the Chamber has admitted it into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Is this a good time for the break as I am about to change topics, or should I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I think it's a good time for a break. Could you give us an indication as to how much time you would still need after the break and perhaps even tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I estimate - and I cut it, given the fact that this is a live testimony - I believe I'll need another hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which means that we cannot finish today. We already -- this already to inform you, Mr. Parsons, that we would very much appreciate your presence tomorrow but not for a very long time. We take a break and we'll resume at a quarter to 2.00, after the witness has left the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Vanderpuye, Mr. Groome is there so I'd like to reserve the last 10 to 15 minutes, depending on how much time Mr. Groome would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just wanted to alert the Chamber that we have the B/C/S translation of P1720, MFI'd. The ERN, the document ID number is 06796805-B/C/ST. And we would ask that the court officer link the translation so that we can admit it at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, leave is granted to link the translation to P1720, and P1720 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I suggest that we -- again, Mr. Groome would -- how much time would you need? I have a few matters as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think ten minutes would take care of my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten minutes. Then we have to stop not any later than 2.00 today to deal with those matters. And since we cannot conclude the testimony of the witness anyhow today, that doesn't make that much of a difference. Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I should like to move on to issues related to DNA methodology and its reach, its scope. Would you agree that DNA methodology could be useful for the reassociation of fragmented mortal remains?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can the DNA method help us establish the time of death of the person whose DNA profile is being analysed?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Generally, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would the DNA method that you use be able to help us establish the way and the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Not directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be possible for a person who is properly identified in your laboratory using the DNA method to have died in another period, not July 1995?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I think that the evidence of the witness is pretty clear about what his tests have resulted in. Now to put a long list of questions to the witness, such as whether the DNA tests could identify whether it was when the person died might not be very useful because the Chamber will limit itself to what the DNA testing in the opinion of this witness has told us. So therefore, could you please keep this in mind when putting further questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, does ICMP have in its possession autopsy reports for the bodies whose DNA samples you analysed?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: We may have some copies, but officially, no, we don't retain those. The ones from PIP would be held there; and that's no longer an ICMP facility, but we have very strong interactions with that facility all along.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell us where physically we could access autopsy reports for these bodies?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I apologise, I don't have that information to provide to you. Autopsies themselves are the purview of the forensic pathologists, not the ICMP scientists.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to conclude that it was precisely on the basis of the conclusions of the forensic pathologists and the autopsy reports that the cause of death could be established with greater certainty for the bodies that you identified?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: Well, I have to delve into the details just a little bit on that. Many of the skeletal -- many of the remains that are dealt with from Srebrenica and other areas of Bosnia are essentially fully skeletonised, which does bring their examination and analysis into the realm of the field of forensic anthropology as opposed to pathology per se. By that I mean most of the true forensic expertise applied to the examination and analysis comes from the work of ICMP anthropologists, and those skeletal reports are part of a forensic management database that the ICMP maintains. And in many instances, trauma is recorded by ICMP anthropologists if those are the cases that they have been involved in examining. So when I say many instances, I mean thousands where they would, for example, note a bullet-hole on the back of the skull or shattered bones consistent with a blast or a high-velocity projectile. Those anthropology reports then are often used in conjunction with or condensed in the autopsy reports that are maintained by the pathologist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I don't know whether there's any translation issue, yes or no, but your question was whether the conclusions of the forensic pathologists and the autopsy reports, that on the basis of those that the cause of death could be established with greater certainty for the bodies that you identified. I never understood that Mr. Parsons was involved in establishing the cause of death, but rather with the identification primarily of the identity of the bodily remains. So therefore, the greater certainty compared to what, greater certainty than what?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I asked that because I understood the professor as saying that within the ICMP there were also forensic pathologists and anthropologists, who also took part in analysing the cause of death. If my understanding is incorrect, then the question was superfluous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which still doesn't answer my question: Greater than on the basis of what? On the basis, you mean, of witness testimonies or is that what you compare it to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although I did not understand that this was the subject of the specific testimony of Mr. Parsons today but rather of other departments of the organisation -- well, you have clarified your question. Is -- do you like -- would you like to add anything, Mr. Parsons, to your previous answer on a question which was not entirely clear to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so. Thank you. I'd be happy to follow-up to additional questioning if I could be of more assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll put the question in this way, Professor. Does the ICMP conduct any investigation into the time and place of death of the persons for whom you do DNA matching and profiling?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I would have to say yes, starting from the very basic premise that we don't work in a vacuum. We've already seen examples of excavation reports that profile in great detail the contents and characteristics of both primary and secondary graves. Moreover, many of our scientists previously worked on ICTY teams and were very well apprised of the evidentiary context in which our work occurs, to include aerial evidence that showed these various sites not existing as graves prior to a particular time and then being created as graves after a very narrow window of time. So we know where we're working. We're able to see the characteristics of the sites. We're able to see the conditions of the bodies coming out of them. Our anthropologists document physical trauma, skeletal damage consistent with cause of death, and assist the court-appointed pathologist at reaching these conclusions. All these -- all this background is the context in which the DNA identifications where we put exact names to the victims of these incidents. So yes, we have a great deal of investigation. We gather evidence, we document it, and it becomes part of the historical record.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please help me understand this. Do the results obtained by the ICMP in themselves provide any information about the cause and manner of death?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS
utterances.text: I would say that when an ICMP physical anthropologist is examining a set of skeletal remains that has a bullet-hole in the back of the head, that they are actually providing information about the cause and manner of death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I'm sorry to interrupt, but we need to deal with a few procedural matters. Mr. Parsons, if we would not have done that, it would not have saved you because we would not have finished anyhow. We would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom. And I would like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether the testimony you gave today or the testimony still to be given tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, before I give you the ten minutes you asked for, I have the following matter to deal with first. The Prosecution's 28th motion to admit evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis was discussed recently and we had not received any response by the 6th of June. On the 8th of July, the OTP stated that it will not object to a request for an extension to respond, and the Defence was granted until the 9th of July, which is today, to ask for an extension. We have not heard from the Defence yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We did not have time this morning, Your Honour, but I can respond to the 28th and the 29th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to do it now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if it can be briefly done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I believe it can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have reviewed our records and located those filings, which we unfortunately have not yet reviewed with the aim of preparing a response. With everything else going on, they could not be processed particularly with the manner in which they were served upon us, in multiple e-mails, out of order, with no name of the motion in the subject, that needed to be downloaded and manually sorted. Hence, we require additional time, particularly in light of the currently pending and filed urgent Prosecution motions pertaining to several of the Prosecution experts that are coming up in the next week -- few weeks that have been filed and which we have been attending to. Including in this is the one that Your Honours have advanced the dead-line for the -- for to be the 10th of July, 2013. We know that there are another four such Rule 92 bis motions for which extensions have been or will be filed and for which we are already working on the responses. Two of those already have a court-ordered new due date. That means that that is a lot already on our plates. We thus ask for 30 [Realtime transcript read in error "three"] days for the 29th -- 28th motion from today's date and 45 days from today's date for the 29th motion's response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any specific --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- any specific explanation for the three days for the one and 45 days for the other?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We need something in between to work on the second one when we finish the first one. Because the first one is, I think, more than 400 pages. And the -- and it's really -- or maybe the second one. I'm not sure now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. You're asking for three days' extension of time --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 30 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 30 days?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understood three days. Then we misunderstood you. That's 30 days for the one. We'll consider it. Any response by the Prosecution at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Other than to note our continued position with respect to these applications. We don't oppose any time that the Chamber believes is reasonable. With respect to what sounds like a problem with the motion itself, if Mr. Lukic speaks with me after court today, I will see that he has the full and correct version of the application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll consider it and we'll let you know. Then, Mr. Groome, we have ten minutes left so that you can make your -- any submissions on matters, I take it the matters we -- the Chamber raised yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yesterday the Chamber posed several questions to the Prosecution and I will answer them now. First the Chamber asked whether it would be possible to file all 92 bis, 92 quater, and bar table motions by the 30th of August. The answer is that we are endeavouring to do this and reasonably expect that we will with the exception of one motion. There are, however, two categories of bar table motions that we will not be able to. The first we await the Chamber's decisions on a number of 92 bis and 92 quater applications that have already been filed. There will be additional 92 bis and quater filings in the coming weeks. In many of these applications, the Prosecution tenders associated exhibits. If the Chamber rejects the 92 bis or quater application in its entirety or in part by excluding some of the associated exhibits, the Prosecution may consider it necessary to tender these documents in bar table motions. The second category of possible bar table motions after the 30th relates to those witnesses who are scheduled to testify after that date. It is our intention to tender documents through some of these witnesses. Of course, if they are rejected, we may consider it necessary to tender them in a bar table motion. The next query the Chamber made of the Prosecution yesterday related to the volume of applications that are still to come as well as some additional information about them. With respect to 92 bis applications, the Prosecution will be filing with the next -- within the next several weeks and in any case prior to August 30th, nine 92 bis motions, one for the Sarajevo component, two for the municipality component, and six for the Srebrenica component. The Chamber will have seen numerous assignments by the Registrar of Legal Officers to officiate the attestation of 92 bis witness statements. That process is underway and is expected to be completed sometime in September. We have in the past notified the Chamber of our intention to not adduce the evidence of 29 witnesses in reliance on this Chamber taking judicial notice of previously adjudicated facts. We did this most recently on the 19th of June. As noted in that filing, we are considering whether prudence requires us to make 92 bis applications with respect to several of these witnesses. Although we have not come to a final view, I think it is likely that we will file such applications for several of them. With respect to 92 quater, the Prosecution still has to file motions for ten witnesses who are unavailable, two for Sarajevo, two for the municipalities, and six for the Srebrenica component. With respect to bar tables, the Prosecution anticipates filing two additional bar table motions this week. One motion with respect to ten audio tapes or excerpts from ten audio tapes recovered from Mr. Mladic's home. The second, a bar table of some documents related to the municipality of Foca. With respect to other potential bar tables, we are working on seven additional bar table motions. The first one tendering a modest number of videos. The second, a municipality bar table motion that will consist of several hundred documents. Third, a military document bar table motion which will several hundred documents. We have already filed a bar table motion with respect to UN reports and Resolutions. We will be supplementing that with another UN report bar table once we have received the necessary translations. CLSS indicates that they will have these translations completed after the break. The Prosecution will also be filing a bar table motion specifically for documents from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. The Prosecution is planning to file this bar table motion prior to the break. The sixth bar table motion will contain several categories of documents related to the Sarajevo component. We anticipate that that will not be ready for filing until September. The Prosecution also anticipates filing a bar table motion for the Srebrenica component of a modest number of documents. In addition to all of the motions referred to already, there are an additional two. The Prosecution will be moving to add a witness to its witness list with respect to our proof on the Sarajevo component of the case. The 92 bis motion for that witness is being prepared in tandem and will be filed immediately after the Chamber decides on our application. The Prosecution will also be making a motion to add several documents we recently received relevant to the proof of death component of our case. The final question put to the Prosecution related to our filing in relation to the expert Reynaud Theunens. The Chamber informed the Prosecution that it would set a dead-line for the 26th of July for that filing. Yesterday morning I received a near final draft of our response. It is a filing that I consider of some importance and we will work to finalise our submission before the end of tomorrow. With respect to the reports of other experts, I assure the Chamber that the Prosecution is working diligently to finalise them as quickly as possible and to file them with the Court. And, Your Honour, I can answer any specific questions the Chamber may have about my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, not only in view of the time but also in view of the magnitude of information provided to us, I think we first need more time to digest all the information you've given us before we are able to put any additional questions. Now may I take it that, Mr. Lukic, that you may need more time as well to -- if you want to respond or make any submissions on what the Prosecution just said? I would not expect you to do that within the next one and a half minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn for the day and we will resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 10th of July, at 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 10th day of July, 2013, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.14 p.m.,
